title: Karpenter's consolidation behaviour is counter-intuitive
excerpt: OK, this story starts off with a colleague messaging me at 9am on a Tuesday morning: “Hey, drmorr, Karpenter is behaving a little bit strangely in this cluster, could you take a quick look?”

OK, this story starts off with a colleague messaging me at 9am on a Tuesday morning: “Hey, drmorr, Karpenter is behaving a little bit strangely in this cluster, could you take a quick look?”

“Sure,” I said, before I’d gotten my morning caffeine. It’ll probably take about 15 minutes and then I can get on with my day, I thought to myself1. Five hours later, I finally understood what was going on. Two hours after that, I understood it well-enough to be able to explain it to my colleague2. A week or so later, I understood it well enough to write this blog post.

Spoiler warning: there’s no bug in Karpenter, and everything in the sequence logically follows from one step to the next, but (at least for me) the outcome was still surprising enough that I thought I’d write a post about it.

So just to be clear, I’ve filed off all the serial numbers on this post to protect… I dunno, probably nobody, I don’t think there’s anything particularly sensitive here, but anyways. The issue started out with a graph that looks like this:

This graph is showing the unused CPUs in a cluster, aggregated by the nodes in the cluster. In other words, each line represents a different node, and the value at any point is the number of available (schedulable) CPUs on that node. It is a stacked graph so that we can get an idea of both the distribution of unused CPUs as well as the total unused CPUs in the cluster.

This graph is pretty hard to read! But, if you squint at it for long enough, two things become apparent: first, the “available CPU capacity” in the cluster is pretty constant: we more-or-less always have 5 CPUs available. And secondly, despite this, nodes in the cluster are churning constantly. This pattern in this graph repeated for well over 12 hours. What??? Why would Karpenter be doing this? Is this even Karpenter’s fault???

However, after checking the Karpenter logs, I was able to confirm that Karpenter was terminating these nodes because of node consolidation. But I’m still very confused: Karpenter is supposed to consolidate nodes to binpack the cluster better—in other words, after a node consolidation event, the “available capacity” in the cluster should decrease! But that’s not what we see: after a node consolidation event, the available capacity stays constant.

To understand what’s happening here, we need to know about two things: what’s running on this cluster, and how Karpenter’s node consolidation works. Let’s first talk about Karpenter node consolidation, because I hear a lot of lies subtly imprecise discussion about how it works3.

The standard sales pitch4 for Karpenter goes like this: “Install this magic autoscaler and all your problems will go away!”

Sorry, that was snarky. Let’s try again. The standard sales pitch for Karpenter goes like this: “Install this magic autoscaler and it will make your cluster much, much cheaper!” That was still snarky5, but is closer to the truth. The question is, “How does Karpenter make things cheaper?” The answer is node consolidation.

At a very high level, Karpenter has two control loops: one is the “scale up” loop and the other is the “consolidation” loop (I wrote about analyzing the performance of these two control loops way back in the SimKube 1.0 days). The scale-up loop is designed to be fast: it responds to any Pending pods very quickly, and launches new nodes to get those pods scheduled ASAP. The consolidation loop is slower; it’s constantly on the hunt for the “optimal” configuration of pods and nodes, where “optimal” in this case means “cheapest”. In practice, what this means is that it is constantly trying to shrink the cluster (aka, bin-pack it) by moving pods off of “lightly used” nodes so that those nodes can be terminated6. In theory, this results in lower cost since you’re not paying AWS for as many compute resources.

Let’s dig into the consolidation behaviour in a bit more detail; if you read the Karpenter docs on this topic, you might be surprised to learn that there are very few knobs you can turn here! You can only set two parameters (on a per-node-pool basis): consolidationPolicy and consolidateAfter. The first parameter controls how Karpenter performs consolidation, and you can either set it to WhenEmpty or WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized7; the second parameter controls how long a node has to sit around before the consolidation mechanism kicks in.

In general, if you’re running Karpenter, you “probably” want to be using WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized; if not, you’re just waiting for pods to naturally cycle out of your cluster before any sort of bin-packing kicks in, and this is in general going to result in a lot of mostly-empty nodes sitting around in your cluster. So really the only parameter that has any meaningful choices is consolidateAfter. This knob helps reduce churn: set it low, and Karpenter will kick nodes out of the cluster extremely rapidly8; but this might be undesirable if you have a new workload coming in that could have used that node. Then you have to spin up a new node, and node provisioning likely takes you longer (and costs you more) than just keeping a “warm” node around in the cluster a bit longer. If you expect this sort of thing to happen regularly, you can set consolidateAfter to a higher value to tell Karpenter to keep nodes around9.

I’ve read through that Karpenter documentation page dozens of times at this point, and every time I’ve read through it, I’ve thought, “It sure is weird that there’s no way to control the utilization threshold for Karpenter’s consolidation behaviour!” In other words, we always talk about Karpenter consolidating “underutilized” nodes, which implies that there is some threshold at which Karpenter considers a node “not underutilized”, and I’ve always been a little surprised that threshold isn’t tunable. But it turns out there’s a very good reason why that threshold isn’t tunable: there is no such threshold.

Specifically: Karpenter will consider a node for consolidation regardless of how full it is. Doesn’t matter if there’s one pod or one hundred pods running on the node, as long as we’re outside the node’s consolidateAfter window, the node is eligible for consolidation. The only10 thing that matters, from Karpenter’s perspective is, “do all these pods fit somewhere else?” If the answer is yes, buh-bye, out you go!

The implication here is that Karpenter’s consolidation behaviour has nothing at all to do with the state of the node in question, and EVERYTHING to do with the state of the cluster around it. A node with a hundred pods in a fully loaded cluster? Won’t get consolidated. That same hundred-pod node in a cluster with lots of other empty nodes? Might get consolidated. Or to put it in even starker terms: Karpenter is using global state (what does the entire cluster look like?) to make a local decision (what should I do with this node?). Generally that is the inverse of what we want in distributed systems.

Now that we (or, at least, I) have a better understanding of Karpenter’s consolidation behaviour, let’s look back at the workloads running on this cluster, and specifically at the graph I shared at the beginning of this post. Does anything seem odd about this graph? I didn’t see it until I looked at the inverse of the graph. Instead of looking at the remaining available capacity in the cluster, let’s look at the committed (scheduled) CPU capacity in the cluster:

This graph is still kinda hard to read, but it’s a little bit easier. We can see that the used capacity in the cluster is more-or-less constant now, even as nodes are churning, but also—huh, look at those spikes11! I wonder what those are? It turns out that in this cluster, there are a number of long-lived pods running on the same node pool as an extremely short-lived Job that a) gets triggered at fairly regular intervals, and b) consumes quite a large amount of compute (relatively speaking). The other important thing to understand is that some of the long-lived pods in the cluster have a termination grace period set, which means that (after Karpenter has marked the node for consolidation) the node will stick around for some period of time before the remaining pods get shuffled off of it.

So now we have all the pieces to understand what’s happening; instead of squinting at stacked timeseries graphs, it will be a little clearer if we draw the nodes and their contents out explicitly. So, consider the following scenario: we have three nodes, A, B, and C with workloads distributed as follows:

At this point, there is no short-lived, resource-heavy pod present, and all of the other pods can fit on two nodes, so Karpenter decides to start consolidating node A:

Most of the pods on node A have been evicted and rescheduled onto node B; one of the pods on node A is still in a “terminating” state while its grace period expires. Now, shortly thereafter, the big, short-lived pod shows up (for the purposes of this example, it takes up an entire node, but it’s trivial to construct cases where it does not). It has no place to run12, so Karpenter launches a new node for it:

Soon thereafter, the short-lived pod finishes, and we now have three active nodes in the cluster again. Nodes B and D are both ineligible for consolidation, because they’ve both had scaling activities recently13; however, node C has just been sitting there for a while! Karpenter can consolidate it! So it does:

And, now we’re back at the beginning of the cycle. This will repeat indefinitely as long as this short-lived, resource-heavy pod continues to appear at regular intervals, and as long as nothing else breaks the cycle. Congratulations! You have introduced constant node churn into your cluster as a consequence of seemingly isolated and independently logical scaling rules.

Well now, that’s the real interesting14 question, isn’t it? How do you fix this? This is the real challenge with autoscaling: you can add in another rule to try to break the cycle, but how do you know that this new rule that you add isn’t going to have other unintended consequences down the line? Basically: you don’t. There is so much emergent behaviour when you try to scale things up and down, and it’s nigh-impossible to reason about all of it.

I know you all are hoping I have a good answer, but I actually don’t. It’s a little bit bonkers that Karpenter has decided, “Hey, I’ve got this fully loaded node, and this mostly empty node over here, but I’m not allowed to touch the mostly empty node, so I’m going to reschedule ALL OF THE PODS on this fully loaded node instead!” But how do you fix this? Here are some options:

  1. Maybe Karpenter should actually have some kind of consolidation threshold for nodes? E.g., if node A is more than 75% full (or it has more than 42 pods as an absolute number), Karpenter won’t touch it. This would prevent nodes with a lot of pods from getting consolidated, but could also prevent the cluster from scaling down when desired.

  2. Karpenter could consider nodes that have had recent scheduling activity as ineligible for other pods during its scheduling simulation15. This could also have significant impacts to its consolidation ability, and is also a significant departure from what kube-scheduler would actually do (edit to add: this has actually been done and is available in Karpenter 1.14)

  3. Maybe Karpenter needs some kind of “global churn threshold”: it kind of has this, with its node pool disruption budgets, but this just takes into account nodes that are being terminated Right Now, and doesn’t look at historical churn rates.

  4. Maybe Karpenter should consider historical usage when making consolidation decisions; in other words, it tries to predict that “oh, this short-lived but resource-intensive pod has been showing up extremely regularly, maybe I should try to leave some room for it.” This would be extremely cool, but predictive autoscaling behaviour is also extremely hard to do, and there’s even more cases where it can go wrong than a purely reactive autoscaler.

There are probably some other potential solutions as will, but which one is right? Maybe you should implement multiple options? But what if they conflict in weird ways with other scaling rules? How do you even know? Most of the time, when faced with an autoscaler problem like this, people make decisions based on extremely rigorous criteria such as “vibes” and “YOLO”.

But man, wouldn’t it be nice if there was a better way?

As always, thanks for reading :)

blocks.html_en: At a very high level, Karpenter has two control loops: one is the “scale up” loop and the other is the “consolidation” loop (I wrote about analyzing the performance of these two control loops way back in the SimKube 1.0 days). The scale-up loop is designed to be fast: it responds to any Pending pods very quickly, and launches new nodes to get those pods scheduled ASAP. The consolidation loop is slower; it’s constantly on the hunt for the “optimal” configuration of pods and nodes, where “optimal” in this case means “cheapest”. In practice, what this means is that it is constantly trying to shrink the cluster (aka, bin-pack it) by moving pods off of “lightly used” nodes so that those nodes can be terminated6. In theory, this results in lower cost since you’re not paying AWS for as many compute resources.

blocks.html_en: Let’s dig into the consolidation behaviour in a bit more detail; if you read the Karpenter docs on this topic, you might be surprised to learn that there are very few knobs you can turn here! You can only set two parameters (on a per-node-pool basis): consolidationPolicy and consolidateAfter. The first parameter controls how Karpenter performs consolidation, and you can either set it to WhenEmpty or WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized7; the second parameter controls how long a node has to sit around before the consolidation mechanism kicks in.

blocks.html_en: In general, if you’re running Karpenter, you “probably” want to be using WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized; if not, you’re just waiting for pods to naturally cycle out of your cluster before any sort of bin-packing kicks in, and this is in general going to result in a lot of mostly-empty nodes sitting around in your cluster. So really the only parameter that has any meaningful choices is consolidateAfter. This knob helps reduce churn: set it low, and Karpenter will kick nodes out of the cluster extremely rapidly8; but this might be undesirable if you have a new workload coming in that could have used that node. Then you have to spin up a new node, and node provisioning likely takes you longer (and costs you more) than just keeping a “warm” node around in the cluster a bit longer. If you expect this sort of thing to happen regularly, you can set consolidateAfter to a higher value to tell Karpenter to keep nodes around9.

blocks.html_en: I’ve read through that Karpenter documentation page dozens of times at this point, and every time I’ve read through it, I’ve thought, “It sure is weird that there’s no way to control the utilization threshold for Karpenter’s consolidation behaviour!” In other words, we always talk about Karpenter consolidating “underutilized” nodes, which implies that there is some threshold at which Karpenter considers a node “not underutilized”, and I’ve always been a little surprised that threshold isn’t tunable. But it turns out there’s a very good reason why that threshold isn’t tunable: there is no such threshold.

blocks.html_en: The implication here is that Karpenter’s consolidation behaviour has nothing at all to do with the state of the node in question, and EVERYTHING to do with the state of the cluster around it. A node with a hundred pods in a fully loaded cluster? Won’t get consolidated. That same hundred-pod node in a cluster with lots of other empty nodes? Might get consolidated. Or to put it in even starker terms: Karpenter is using global state (what does the entire cluster look like?) to make a local decision (what should I do with this node?). Generally that is the inverse of what we want in distributed systems.

好吧，这个故事是从一位同事在周二早上 9 点给我发消息开始的：“嘿，dmorr，卡彭特在这个集群中的行为有点奇怪，你能快速看一下吗？”

“当然，”我在早上喝咖啡之前说道。 我心里想，这可能需要大约 15 分钟，然后我就可以继续我的一天了。 五个小时后，我终于明白是怎么回事了。 两个小时后，我已经完全理解了，可以向我的同事解释了。 大约一周后，我充分理解了它，写了这篇博文。

剧透警告：《Karpenter》中没有错误，序列中的所有内容都按逻辑从一步到下一步，但（至少对我来说）结果仍然足够令人惊讶，我想我应该写一篇关于它的文章。

因此，为了清楚起见，我已将这篇文章中的所有序列号归档以保护...... 我不知道，可能没有人，我不认为这里有什么特别敏感的东西，但无论如何。 该问题始于一个如下图所示的图表：

该图显示了集群中未使用的 CPU，由集群中的节点聚合。 换句话说，每条线代表一个不同的节点，任意点的值都是该节点上可用（可调度）CPU 的数量。 它是一个堆叠图，因此我们可以了解集群中未使用 CPU 的分布以及未使用 CPU 的总数。

这张图很难读！ 但是，如果你仔细观察它足够长的时间，有两件事就会变得显而易见：首先，集群中的“可用 CPU 容量”相当恒定：我们或多或少总是有 5 个可用的 CPU。 其次，尽管如此，集群中的节点仍在不断地变动。 该图中的这种模式重复了 12 个多小时。 什么？？？ 卡彭特为什么要这么做？ 这也是卡彭特的错吗？？？

但是，在检查 Karpenter 日志后，我能够确认 Karpenter 由于节点合并而终止了这些节点。 但我仍然很困惑：Karpenter 应该整合节点以更好地对集群进行 binpack——换句话说，在节点整合事件之后，集群中的“可用容量”应该减少！ 但这不是我们所看到的：在节点合并事件之后，可用容量保持不变。

要了解这里发生的情况，我们需要了解两件事：该集群上正在运行什么，以及 Karpenter 的节点整合如何工作。 让我们首先谈谈 Karpenter 节点整合，因为我听到很多关于它如何工作的谎言，微妙地不精确的讨论3。

卡彭特的标准销售宣传4是这样的：“安装这个神奇的自动缩放器，你所有的问题都会消失！”

抱歉，这太尖酸刻薄了。 我们再试一次。 Karpenter 的标准销售宣传是这样的：“安装这个神奇的自动缩放器，它将使您的集群便宜得多！” 这仍然是尖刻的5，但更接近事实。 问题是，“卡彭特如何让东西变得更便宜？” 答案是节点整合。

在非常高的层面上，Karpenter 有两个控制循环：一个是“扩展”循环，另一个是“整合”循环（我早在 SimKube 1.0 时代就写过分析这两个控制循环性能的文章）。 扩展循环的设计速度很快：它会非常快速地响应任何待处理的 Pod，并启动新节点以尽快安排这些 Pod。 整合循环速度较慢；它不断寻找 Pod 和节点的“最佳”配置，在这种情况下，“最佳”意味着“最便宜”。 实际上，这意味着它不断尝试通过将 Pod 从“轻度使用”节点上移出来缩小集群（也称为装箱），以便可以终止这些节点6。 从理论上讲，这会降低成本，因为您无需向 AWS 支付尽可能多的计算资源费用。

让我们更详细地研究一下合并行为；如果您阅读有关此主题的 Karpenter 文档，您可能会惊讶地发现这里可以转动的旋钮非常少！ 您只能设置两个参数（基于每个节点池）：consolidatePolicy 和 consolidateAfter。 第一个参数控制 Karpenter 如何执行合并，您可以将其设置为 WhenEmpty 或 WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized7；第二个参数控制在整合机制启动之前节点必须停留的时间。

一般来说，如果您正在运行 Karpenter，您“可能”希望使用 WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized；如果没有，您只是在等待 Pod 在任何类型的装箱开始之前自然地循环出集群，这通常会导致集群中出现大量大部分为空的节点。 因此，唯一具有任何有意义选择的参数是 consolidateAfter。 该旋钮有助于减少流失：将其设置得较低，Karpenter 会极快地将节点踢出集群8；但如果您有一个可能使用该节点的新工作负载进入，这可能是不可取的。 然后，您必须启动一个新节点，而节点配置可能比仅在集群中保留“热”节点更长时间（并且成本更高）。 如果您预计这种情况会定期发生，则可以将 consolidateAfter 设置为更高的值，以告诉 Karpenter 将节点保持在 9 左右。

此时，我已经通读了 Karpenter 文档页面数十次，每次通读它时，我都会想：“没有办法控制 Karpenter 合并行为的利用率阈值，这确实很奇怪！” 换句话说，我们总是谈论 Karpenter 整合“未充分利用”的节点，这意味着存在某个阈值，在该阈值下，Karpenter 认为节点“未充分利用”，而我总是对阈值不可调整感到有点惊讶。 但事实证明，这个阈值不可调节有一个很好的理由：不存在这样的阈值。

具体来说：无论节点有多满，Karpenter 都会考虑进行合并。 无论节点上运行 1 个 pod 还是 100 个 pod，只要我们位于节点的 consolidateAfter 窗口之外，该节点就有资格进行整合。 从卡彭特的角度来看，唯一重要的事情是“所有这些吊舱都适合其他地方吗？” 如果答案是肯定的，再见，你走吧！

这里的含义是，Karpenter 的整合行为与相关节点的状态完全无关，而与它周围的集群的状态有关。 满载的集群中有一百个 Pod 的节点？ 不会被合并。 集群中是否有相同的一百个 Pod 节点以及许多其他空节点？ 可能会合并。 或者用更严厉的话说：Karpenter 正在使用全局状态（整个集群是什么样子？） 做出本地决策（我应该如何处理这个节点？）。 一般来说，这与我们在分布式系统中想要的相反。

现在我们（或者至少是我）对 Karpenter 的整合行为有了更好的了解，让我们回顾一下在这个集群上运行的工作负载，特别是我在本文开头分享的图表。 这张图有什么奇怪的地方吗？ 直到我查看了图的反转后我才发现这一点。 我们不再查看集群中的剩余可用容量，而是查看集群中已提交（计划）的 CPU 容量：

这张图仍然有点难以阅读，但它更容易一些。 我们可以看到，即使节点在搅动，集群中的已用容量现在或多或少是恒定的，而且 - 嗯，看看那些峰值11！ 我想知道那些是什么？ 事实证明，在这个集群中，有许多长期生存的 Pod 在同一个节点池上运行，作为一个极其短期的作业，a）以相当规律的时间间隔触发，b）消耗相当大量的计算（相对而言）。 另一件需要理解的重要事情是，集群中的一些长期存在的 Pod 设置了终止宽限期，这意味着（在 Karpenter 将节点标记为合并之后）该节点将保留一段时间，然后剩余的 Pod 才会被清除。

现在我们已经掌握了了解正在发生的事情的所有信息；如果我们明确地绘制节点及其内容，而不是眯着眼睛看堆叠的时间序列图，它会更清晰一些。 因此，考虑以下场景：我们有三个节点 A、B 和 C，工作负载分布如下：

此时，不存在生命周期短、占用大量资源的 pod，并且所有其他 pod 都可以安装在两个节点上，因此 Karpenter 决定开始整合节点 A：

节点 A 上的大部分 Pod 已被驱逐并重新调度到节点 B 上；节点 A 上的一个 Pod 在其宽限期到期时仍处于“终止”状态。 现在，不久之后，大的、短命的 pod 出现了（就本示例而言，它占用了整个节点，但构建不占用整个节点的情况很简单）。 它没有地方运行12，所以 Karpenter 为它启动了一个新节点：

此后不久，短暂的 Pod 就会结束，现在集群中又拥有了三个活动节点。 节点 B 和 D 都没有资格进行整合，因为它们最近都有扩容活动13；然而，节点 C 刚刚在那里呆了一段时间！ 卡彭特可以巩固它！ 所以它确实：

而且，现在我们又回到了周期的开始。 只要这个短暂的、资源密集型的 Pod 继续定期出现，并且只要没有其他东西打破这个循环，这种情况就会无限期地重复。 恭喜！ 由于看似孤立且独立的逻辑扩展规则，您已经在集群中引入了持续的节点流失。

好吧，这才是真正有趣的问题，不是吗？ 你如何解决这个问题？ 这是自动缩放的真正挑战：您可以添加另一条规则来尝试打破循环，但是您如何知道您添加的这条新规则不会产生其他意想不到的后果？ 基本上：你不知道。 当你试图放大或缩小事物时，会出现很多突发行为，而且几乎不可能对所有这些进行推理。

我知道你们都希望我有一个好的答案，但实际上我没有。 Karpenter 的决定有点疯狂，“嘿，我已经有了这个满载的节点，这里还有一个大部分为空的节点，但我不允许触及大部分为空的节点，所以我要在这个满载的节点上重新安排所有的 Pod！” 但如何解决这个问题呢？ 以下是一些选项：

  1. 也许卡彭特实际上应该为节点设置某种整合阈值？ 例如，如果节点 A 的填充率超过 75%（或者其绝对数量超过 42 个 Pod），Karpenter 就不会碰它。 这将阻止具有大量 Pod 的节点进行整合，但也可能阻止集群在需要时缩小规模。
  2. Karpenter 可以在调度模拟期间将最近进行过调度活动的节点视为没有资格参与其他 Pod15。 这也可能对其整合能力产生重大影响，并且也与 kube-scheduler 实际执行的操作存在重大偏差（编辑添加：这实际上已经完成并且在 Karpenter 1.14 中可用）
  3. 也许 Karpenter 需要某种“全局流失阈值”：它有这样的设置，包括节点池中断预算，但这只是考虑了现在正在终止的节点，而不考虑历史流失率。
  4. 也许卡彭特在做出整合决策时应该考虑历史使用情况；换句话说，它试图预测“哦，这个短暂但资源密集的 Pod 已经非常频繁地出现，也许我应该尝试为它留出一些空间。” 这将是非常酷的，但预测性自动缩放行为也非常难以做到，而且比纯粹的反应式自动缩放器更有可能出错的情况。

可能还有其他一些潜在的解决方案，但哪一个是正确的呢？ 也许您应该实施多个选项？ 但如果它们以奇怪的方式与其他缩放规则发生冲突怎么办？ 你怎么知道？ 大多数时候，当面对这样的自动缩放器问题时，人们会根据极其严格的标准（例如“vibes”和“YOLO”）做出决策。

但是伙计，如果有更好的方法不是更好吗？

一如既往，感谢您的阅读:)

〜drmorr
